text.text: Objective: Assess which architecture is the most label-efficient for vessel segmentation of catheter-based angiograms, and whether a diffusion model trained with extreme data scarcity could serve as a scaffold for expert annotation.

Materials and Methods: x0-diffusion, SAM, DeepLabV3, ResNet-UNet, ViT-DPT, and ResNet-ViT hybrid were compared at 16, 32, and 80 labeled images from the 500-image Dr-SAM dataset under 5×5-fold repeated cross-validation, using one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction.
A vascular surgeon's annotation time, from scratch and when correcting x0-diffusion predictions, was also measured.

Results: At 16 training images, x0-diffusion achieved the highest Dice (0.882) and IoU (0.795) of the six models, outperforming every competitor in all 25 paired runs on Dice, by 0.047 over zero-shot SAM and 0.226 over DeepLabV3.

The advantage narrowed as labels increased: at 32 images x0-diffusion was not significantly different from the two strongest convolutional models, and at 80 images those models scored marginally higher (0.923 and 0.920 vs.
Correcting 16-image x0-diffusion predictions on five test angiograms averaged 11.1 surgeon-minutes per image versus 20.6 from scratch.
Discussion: The advantage of x0-diffusion is label efficiency, not peak accuracy, with the strongest convolutional models needing twice the labels to match it.
It rarely fails where zero-shot SAM fails, so at the start of an annotation campaign, correcting its predicted masks could cut surgeon annotation time by an estimated 37 to 45%.
Conclusion: With very few labels, x0-parameterized diffusion is the strongest vessel segmenter tested and a candidate scaffold for expert annotation.

In the United States, peripheral artery disease (PAD) affects an estimated 10 to 12 million adults over the age of 40 years (and nearly 236 million people worldwide). 1 Catheter-based angiography (CbA) uses x-rays to visualize contrast dye that is injected into blood vessels and plays a unique role in the diagnosis and treatment of PAD.
text.formatted: In the United States, peripheral artery disease (PAD) affects an estimated 10 to 12 million adults over the age of 40 years (and nearly 236 million people worldwide). <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> Catheter-based angiography (CbA) uses x-rays to visualize contrast dye that is injected into blood vessels and plays a unique role in the diagnosis and treatment of PAD.

text.text: As a diagnostic study, CbA remains the gold-standard for definitive diagnosis particularly in cases of diagnostic uncertainty.
CbA facilitates operative planning due to its ability to reliably resolve blood vessels below the knee and simultaneously provide both anatomic and physiologic data.
These attributes make it vital in assessing target vessels for surgical bypass.

Finally, CbA serves as an interventional platform for numer-ous intraarterial interventions including balloon angioplasty, stent placement, lithotripsy, atherectomy, "over the wire" embolectomy, and catheter directed thrombolysis. [1] [2] [3]

text.text: Despite high clinical value and wide availability of raw images, CbA remains a largely untapped data source and unexplored modality in machine learning for multiple reasons.
First, there is significant variation in label quality and terminology.
Second, images are not routinely annotated in a way that is easily digestible by machine learning pipelines (i.e. "arrow signs").

Finally, angiographic interpretation requires specialized training and is only routinely performed by three relatively small specialties (vascular surgery, interventional cardiology, interventional radiology).

Our ability to capitalize on the rich clinical information contained in angiography studies is constrained by cost, time, and scarcity of experts. 4, 5 This "annotation bottleneck" remains the critical gap in developing meaningful image-based clinical decision support for PAD.

text.text: In other domains progress is often limited by model capabilities.
In contrast, for advancing AI-enhanced PAD care, we are limited by the efficiency of end-to-end annotation to inference pipelines.

With advances in computer vision, several published works address how to handle imaging based tasks where data constraints are an issue. 6, 7 For our paper, we explore label-efficient segmentation to identify vessels within CbAs.

text.text: This involves providing a limited set of annotated examples in order to learn a new classification of a structure within an image.

A related setting, few-shot segmentation, which learns a new class from a small support set at inference time, has seen several advances over the past few years. 8 A notable one is Meta's Segment Anything Model (SAM), a generalized segmentation model driven by input prompts such as points or bounding boxes, 9 which has been adapted to the medical domain. 10 However, it still requires manual prompts, which cannot be reused for downstream ML tasks, and it struggles to capture complex arterial branching as seen in CbAs. 11, 12 Diffusion models have been responsible for some of the state of the art image generation tasks. 13, 14 Instead of treating segmentation as a discriminative task, the problem is reformulated as a generative task.

The architectures were chosen to span a range of inductive biases highly relevant to label-efficient segmentation.
ResNet-UNet, a convolutional model, has strong local context; at the other end, ViT-DPT, a transformer, has global context.
All are compared to an iterative refinement diffusion model with the x 0 parameterization as its target.

The diffusion model takes a 4-channel input, broken down into a 1-channel noisy mask concatenated with the 3-channel clean angiogram, which is the conditioning signal.
The model architecture is based on the UNet2DModel, 21 which has channel sizes of (64, 128, 256, 512) as a trade-off between capacity and computecost.

The final prediction is thresholded at 0.5 to produce the binary mask on which all metrics are computed.

text.text: We propose three hypotheses, of which only the third is partly tested here (the prediction target ablation).

Firstly, corrupting the mask for 1000 timesteps provides the network with exposure to a wide range of reconstruction problems, while predicting the clean mask directly means that they become tasks of reconstructing vascular structures rather than predicting denoising patterns.
This matters most at 16 training images, where the other networks see too little variety to learn from and the corruption procedure works as a form of implicit regularization.
Secondly, iterative denoising of the mask with conditioning on the image at each step gives the model many opportunities to correct the mistakes made locally, as opposed to a single forward pass.

Thirdly, the x 0 parameterization allows for the use of structure-aware loss functions, such as the Dice + BCE combined loss employed, making the training signal more geometrically consistent with the mask itself.
The diffusion UNet also has more parameters than either convolutional baseline (Methods), so lower capacity does not explain its advantage at 16 images.
The ϵ-prediction variant performed far worse than every other model at every fraction (Results).
We attribute this to the MSE loss rather than to the ϵ parameterization itself.
A noise objective will result in a uniform loss gradient across the whole image and will not create any sharp boundary line between the vessels and the background.

SegDiff and MedSegDiff train with ϵ-prediction successfully, 16, 17 and so under a larger training budget the gap would likely narrow; under our matched budget, x 0 prediction is what allows Dice and BCE to be applied, and we recommend it for diffusion-based segmentation of fine vascular structure.

Several issues limit the conclusions of this study.

The first is the dataset, Dr-SAM covers one modality, one anatomical region (the infrarenal aorta and iliac arteries), and two centers, and its distribution is narrow, so the data efficiency of x 0 -diffusion may not transfer to other vessels, regions, or modalities, including the belowknee arteries where CbA has the most diagnostic value.

Most Dr-SAM images are natively 386 × 448, and the 50 that are 819 × 950 scored no worse after downsampling (mean Dice within 0.014 of the smaller images for every model at every training-set size), so the 384 × 384 input forced by ViT compatibility cost little here, though other resolutions could shift the trends.
Second, the sample, the n = 25 runs in each cell reuse the same 500 images under different partitions and are not independent, and the primary tests are one-sided in favor of x 0 -diffusion.
As noted in Results, a two-sided test finds no significant difference at 32 or 80 images in either direction (Supplementary Table S1).

text.text: However, the trend across sizes is confounded.
When the baselines improve from 16 to 32 images they receive both twice the labels and twice the updates, so our data cannot separate label efficiency from tolerance of a short optimization budget.

text.text: The timing study is a pilot, and as stated before, it used five images chosen to span prediction quality and one surgeon.
Both conditions used the same images.

Four corrections were made 10 days before the fromscratch masks, and all five images had been seen in the discarded first session, so familiarity favored the fromscratch condition and the measured saving is probably conservative.
For the same reason the two masks of each image are not independent, and their agreement may partly reflect anchoring to the model's mask.
They were compared only with each other, not with the Dr-SAM reference.
The correction time for the lowest-scoring image comes from a repeat, and lead times include inspection and any idle time.
The projection assumes that the mean times hold across a campaign.
The comparison set was chosen to isolate inductive bias under matched conditions rather than to benchmark the strongest available system for this task, and three omissions follow from that.
All encoders except SAM were randomly initialized, so ImageNet or medical pretrained convolutional baselines, which a laboratory would use in practice, may close the 16-image gap.
We did not use any data augmentation, which may have adversely affected the performance of discriminative models more than a diffusion model, which implicitly involves perturbing the mask.

Dedicated diffusion-based segmentation frameworks like SegDiff, MedSegDiff, 16, 17 and even foundational models like MedSAM 10 finetuned or prompted for a particular task were not implemented in this work.

text.text: Comparing to them, along with pretraining and augmentation, is the next natural study.
The data show that x 0 -diffusion is the best performing architecture for label efficiency in angiogram segmentation, and this holds across all 25 paired experiments on Dice.

Its lead fades as more labels are introduced, so this, together with its resistance to the catastrophic failures of zero-shot SAM, means that its best use case is as a bootstrapping step in an aggressive labeling campaign.

In a five-image pilot, correcting its predictions took a vascular surgeon 46% less time than annotating from scratch, which projects to 37% to 45% fewer surgeon-hours over campaigns of 80 to 500 labels.
